items.title: A limit game
items.prose: Eight turns on the sum of two dice. Size 1 or 2, width 1 to 3, limit 3 either way. Stop one fill short of the limit: move that side more than £1 from fair, where nobody trades.
items.question: Finish with a P&L of at least £1.50 and no rule breaks.

schedule.text: A market on the sum of two dice, rolled at the end. Fair is £7. Your limit is 3 lots either way. Other traders deal only within £1 of fair.

feedback.correct: You kept inside the limit and still traded.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the size at 1 and watch your room on the side that keeps trading.

byKey.low: Your P&L is under £1.50. Quote within £1 of fair so other traders deal with you.
byKey.crossed: Your bid met or passed your ask, so nobody traded.
byKey.limit: A quote was larger than your room on one side. At short 3, any ask is a break.

explain.text: The model sold 2 at 8 to early buyers, then raised its ask to 8.5, out of reach. It bought 1 at 6 on turn 8. Short 1 with cash +£10 settled at 8: +£2.

items.prose: Limit 3 lots either way. You are long 2.
items.question: How many lots can you sell?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Room to sell is $L + q$.

byKey.buy: That is your room to buy, $3 - 2$.
byKey.limit: You ignored the 2 you hold. Selling them first is free room.

explain.text: Selling 2 takes you flat, and 3 more takes you to −3. Room to sell is $3 + 2 = 5$. Room to buy is only 1.

items.prose: A bet wins with chance 0.55 at evens. Your bankroll is £400.
items.question: What is the Kelly stake, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. At evens $f^* = p - (1 - p)$.

byKey.p: You staked the win chance, 0.55. Subtract the losing chance.
byKey.all: You staked everything because the bet has an edge. One loss ends the game.

explain.text: $f^* = 0.55 - 0.45 = 0.1$, and $0.1 \times 400 = 40$. The stake follows the bankroll up and down. That is why the bankroll never reaches zero.

items.prose: A coin lands your way with chance 0.6 at evens. A friend stakes 40% of the bankroll each bet, twice the Kelly fraction.
items.question: Over many bets, what happens to their bankroll?

options.text: It tends to shrink: the growth a bet is slightly negative
It grows twice as fast as Kelly
options.why: You assumed growth scales with the stake. Past $f^*$ the curve falls, and at 0.4 it is below zero.

options.text: It grows as fast as Kelly, with more swings
options.why: You assumed only the risk changes. The typical growth falls too.
A fraction below 1 never stakes everything, so it cannot reach zero exactly.

byKey.double: You assumed growth scales with the stake. Past $f^*$ the curve falls, and at 0.4 it is below zero.

explain.text: $g(0.4) = 0.6\ln 1.4 + 0.4\ln 0.6 = -0.0024$ a bet. Each bet still has positive expected value. The typical path shrinks all the same.

items.prose: You hold A, which moves 3% a day. B moves 1.5% a day, with correlation 0.6.
items.question: How many units of B do you sell per unit of A?

byKey.inv: You put B's sd on top. A is what you hedge.

explain.text: $h = 0.6 \times 3/1.5 = 1.2$. B moves half as much as A, so you need more of it. The correlation scales that back.

items.prose: A moves 2% a day. Its best hedge has correlation 0.9 with it.
items.question: What daily sd is left after the best hedge, in per cent? Give 2 places.

byKey.var: You scaled by $1 - \rho^2$. Take its square root for the sd.
byKey.lin: You scaled by $1 - \rho$. Square the correlation first.

explain.text: $1 - 0.81 = 0.19$ and $\sqrt{0.19} = 0.436$, so $2\% \times 0.436 = 0.87\%$. Even a correlation of 0.9 leaves over 40% of the sd. Near-perfect hedges are rarer than they sound.

items.prose: Three dice, fair 10.5, your quote 9.5 at 11.5. The interviewer sells you 2 at 9.5.
items.question: Which reply scores best?

options.text: "Long 2 at 9.5; at fair 10.5 I am up £2. A seller may know something and I am long, so I move down: 8.5 at 10.5."

options.why: You gave the quote with no position, P&L or reason.

options.text: "Long 2, up £2. I move up to 10.5 at 12.5."
options.why: You moved the wrong way. Long 2 wants to sell, so the quote moves down.
You apologised for a trade with £2 of edge at fair.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Say the position and P&L, then move down with the reason.

explain.text: Long 2 bought at 9.5 against 10.5 is +£2. A seller is information and the long is risk; both say move down. One sentence carries all of it.

items.prose: A game's blotter: sold 2 at 23, then bought 1 at 19. The true value is 17.
items.question: What is the game's P&L, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add each trade's edge against 17.

byKey.sale: You counted only the sale. The buy at 19 lost 2.
byKey.sign: You counted the buy as a gain. Paying 19 for 17 loses.

explain.text: The sale earns $2 \times 6 = 12$ and the buy loses 2, so the P&L is +£10. You end short 1 at the value 17. The buy at 19 is the trade to ask about in a review.

items.prose: Three cards from a full deck, ace 1 to king 13. The first card shows a 2.
items.question: What is the fair value of the sum? Give 2 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The unseen cards average $362/51$.

byKey.seven: You used 7 for each unseen card. The 2 left the deck, so they average $362/51$.
byKey.deck52: You divided by 52. Only 51 cards are left.

explain.text: The deck now holds $364 - 2 = 362$ points in 51 cards, 7.10 each. Two of them plus the 2 give $2 + 724/51 = 16.20$. A low card out pushes the rest up.

items.prose: After a game, a candidate says: "I made £13, so my quotes were better than the model's £12.50."
items.question: What is wrong with that review?

options.text: It grades one outcome, not the quotes or the risk carried

options.why: You judged by one draw. A different last card reverses the order.

options.text: The gap is too small to matter
options.why: Even a large gap would be one draw. The review should grade the quotes.
Luck is the point: the P&L mixes skill and luck, so review the quotes.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A P&L is one draw from the cards.

explain.text: The £13 run ended short 2, twice the model's risk, and won because the last card was low. With a king as the last card it would have lost £3, against the model's +£4.50. Review the quotes and the position.
